analysis.one_liner: Bans auto insurers from using credit scores, education, job, zip code, and gender to set rates.
analysis.headline: Introduced with zero cosponsors, the bill was sent to the Senate Banking Committee and died there without a hearing or vote when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred private passenger auto insurers — and their affiliate companies — from setting rates or deciding eligibility based on gender, education, occupation, employment status, home ownership, zip code, census tract, marital status, credit score, consumer reports, or prior insurance history. It would have required insurers to make their underwriting rules and rate filings public, and given the FTC, state attorneys general, and individual consumers tools to sue violators. It never advanced past its initial referral to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers who today pay more because of factors unrelated to how they drive: people with low or no credit scores, renters, the unemployed and underemployed, people without college degrees, single or widowed drivers, and people living in certain zip codes or census tracts. The bill's findings argue insurers use these "income proxies" to charge lower-income drivers more while steering affluent drivers to cheaper affiliate policies — and since liability insurance is mandatory in 49 states, drivers cannot simply opt out. It would also help any consumer wanting to inspect how their rate is actually calculated, by stripping trade-secret protection from underwriting rules and rate filings.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income drivers, renters, and those with poor credit

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for auto insurers or their affiliates to use gender, education level, occupation, employment status, home ownership, zip code or adjacent zip codes, census tract, marital status, credit score or credit-based insurance score, consumer reports, previous insurer, or prior purchase history in deciding eligibility or calculating rates — even when a factor merely blocks a consumer from the lowest rate or a discount.

The bill's findings state that insurance is mandatory in every state but New Hampshire, with penalties including fines, license suspension, and imprisonment, so drivers cannot avoid the pricing system; they also state that use of income proxies has become commonplace and results in higher rates for lower-income drivers while affluent drivers get lower rates through affiliate companies.
Requires all underwriting rules and rate filings to be open to public inspection and not treated as proprietary trade secrets, letting consumers and regulators see how prices are actually set.

Creates layered enforcement: FTC civil penalties of at least $2,500 per violation, private consumer lawsuits with actual and punitive damages plus attorneys' fees for willful violations, and state attorneys general suits on behalf of residents.
The FTC could enforce violations as unfair or deceptive acts or practices, and the Act takes effect one year after enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Auto insurers bear the direct cost: they would lose rating variables they currently use to segment customers, could face FTC penalties, consumer lawsuits, and state enforcement, and would have to publish rating rules they now keep as trade secrets. Some drivers would also pay more in relative terms — those with strong credit, homeowners, married drivers, and college-educated drivers currently receive discounts under these factors, and insurers would have to rebuild rates around driving-related measures. Courts and the FTC would carry new enforcement workload.
analysis.who_pays_short: Auto insurers and some good-credit, homeowner drivers

drawbacks.text: Insurers use these variables because their data shows they correlate with losses and profitability; the bill's own findings acknowledge insurers treat them as 'actuarially supported.' Banning them means drivers who currently benefit from credit, homeowner, marital, or education discounts could see premiums rise, so part of the bill is a redistribution of premiums between groups of drivers rather than a pure saving.

The bill would eliminate trade-secret protection for all underwriting rules and rate filings — a step insurers would argue hands competitors their pricing strategies; the bill text explicitly overrides that trade-secret treatment.

It layers federal FTC enforcement and private lawsuits on top of a business regulated by state insurance commissioners, and it preempts state law only where inconsistent — creating potential overlap and litigation over which rules apply.

The safe-harbor provision means no one is liable if they show they maintained 'reasonable procedures to assure compliance,' which could blunt enforcement against insurers that adopt weak internal controls.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a real and well-documented pricing practice: insurers charging more based on income proxies like credit scores, education, and zip codes in a product every driver is legally required to buy. The main honest cost is distributional — rates would shift away from drivers penalized by those proxies and toward some who currently profit from them, and insurers would lose pricing tools their data supports. The public-disclosure and enforcement provisions add compliance and litigation burden, and the reasonable-procedures safe harbor could soften the rules' bite. On balance the consumer-protection upside is substantial; the costs are mostly a redistribution that the bill's authors judged unfair rather than a drag on the economy.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or any vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker introduced the Prohibit Auto Insurance Discrimination Act on September 29, 2020, near the end of the 116th Congress.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee the same day; no further action appears in the record.
No senator from either party signed on as a cosponsor during the bill's lifetime.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill expired in committee without a hearing or vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Auto insurers keep their current rating models — including credit-based scoring and zip-code pricing — with no federal restriction, no new disclosure requirement, and no exposure to FTC or consumer lawsuits. Credit-data companies keep selling credit-based insurance scores. Drivers affected by income-proxy pricing are exactly where they were.

for.name: Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made the case in its findings that income proxies shift insurance costs onto lower-income drivers; the bill attracted no cosponsors.

against.name: Mike Crapo
against.role: Chairman, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup after it was referred to the committee; it died there.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a floor vote and drew zero cosponsors from either party, so the partisan split was never tested — the only recorded support was its Democratic sponsor.

industries.note: Insurers would lose a dozen rating and eligibility variables — including credit scores, education, occupation, and zip code — that let them charge more to lower-income customers while steering affluent customers to cheaper affiliate policies. They would also face public disclosure of rate filings, FTC penalties, and consumer and state lawsuits.
The bill specifically bans credit scores and credit-based insurance scores — a product line the credit bureaus sell to auto insurers — eliminating that market channel.
The bill creates private lawsuits with actual damages, punitive damages for willful violations, and mandatory attorneys' fees for successful consumers, opening a new practice area.
